notes.body:
The passage makes a compelling argument for soul-vision (رؤية النفس) over naked-eye sighting (رؤية الطبع), but it does **not derive a formula that produces "two days" as a fixed or universal gap**. That number was tied to year 400 AH, where the Imam's command from the Pure Presence determined that fasting should begin two days before the community sighted the crescent — defended on principle, not worked backwards from calculation.

The astronomical principle the text does lay out is this: **the moon's separation from the sun** after their conjunction (الاجتماع) is the real cause that makes fasting obligatory. At conjunction, the illuminated half of the moon faces away from the earth. As the moon begins to pull away, light appears along its edge — but the sun's own radiance acts as a barrier (حجاب), blinding the eye to that thin crescent, just as it hides the stars in daylight. An eclipse reduces the sun's light and the stars reappear — the crescent is not absent; it is simply overwhelmed.

There is therefore always **a real, measurable lag between the moment the moon separates from the sun** — which calculation (الحساب) can pinpoint — and the moment the crescent clears enough of that light for the naked eye. That lag is not a fixed number; it shifts each month depending on the geometry of the conjunction, the moon's speed, its angle to the ecliptic, and the observer's latitude. For year 400 AH, it came to two days. The Imam, whose knowledge is soul-vision at its most exalted, commanded fasting from the moment the cause was established — not from the moment its effect became visible to an eye that can be deceived by light, cloud, or distance.

etymology: الاجتماع (conjunction): from root ج-م-ع, to gather, collect, or unite. اجتماع is the verbal noun of the Form VIII verb اجتمع — "they came together." In astronomy it names the moment the moon and sun occupy the same degree: two luminaries gathered at one point before separating into their distinct paths.

رؤية (vision/sighting): from root ر-أ-ي, to see or behold. رؤية is the verbal noun — "the act of seeing." The root carries both physical sight and mental perception, which is why the argument works: the same word covers eye-vision and soul-vision, making the distinction between them linguistically inescapable.

الحجاب (barrier/veil): from root ح-ج-ب, to screen, conceal, or prevent access. حجاب is whatever stands between the eye and the thing it seeks. Here it names the sun's overpowering light that hides the crescent — the same word used for the veil separating the mortal world from the divine.

الحساب (calculation/reckoning): from root ح-س-ب, to count or reckon. الحساب is the reckoning — the same word the Quran uses both for the Day of Reckoning and for astronomical precision: "so that you might know the number of the years and the reckoning." Divine judgment and mathematical calculation share one root.

الهلال (crescent): from root ه-ل-ل, whose core sense is a joyful cry or the gleam of something new. الهلال names the crescent — not for its shape but for the shout that greeted its appearance each month. The root also gives هلّل, the cry of divine praise, so the crescent carries within its very name a note of spiritual joy.

notes.body:
The author does not claim inference is independent of the senses altogether. His argument is more precise: **the soul needs the senses only at the first moment of contact**. When the soul receives the image of a thing for the first time, it stores that image within itself. After that, it works from what it holds — not from fresh sensory reports vulnerable to distortion.

Beyond that first moment, the soul and the eye operate in entirely different domains. The eye apprehends qualities — color, shape, thickness — that fluctuate with conditions like distance, light, and obstruction. Soul-vision (رؤية النفس) operates in the domain of **necessary causal and mathematical relations**, where those fluctuations cannot reach. If a drop is removed from a pool, the soul judges with certainty that the water has decreased by exactly that measure.

The crescent makes this concrete. What actually needs to be established is a positional fact: has the moon separated from the sun and moved to the west of it? Even when every obstruction is lifted, the eye apprehends only color and shape — it never directly apprehends a positional relationship. The sun's light blocks the eye from seeing the crescent; it cannot block the soul from knowing that **the conjunction has passed and the new month has begun** by mathematical necessity.

The Quran gives this capacity a name — inference (استنباط), from a root meaning to draw hidden water up from a well:

وَلَوْ رَدُّوهُ إِلَى ٱلرَّسُولِ وَإِلَىٰٓ أُو۟لِى ٱلْأَمْرِ مِنْهُمْ لَعَلِمَهُ ٱلَّذِينَ يَسْتَنۢبِطُونَهُۥ مِنْهُمْ
"Had they referred it to the Messenger and to those charged with authority among them, those among them who draw out conclusions would have known it."
An-Nisa 4:83
notes.anchor: the seeing of knowledge scarcely errs in what it encompasses
notes.quote: the seeing of knowledge scarcely errs in what it encompasses
etymology: رؤية (vision): from the root ر-أ-ي, meaning to see or directly apprehend. The noun رؤية names 'a seeing.' Crucially, the text applies the same word to both eye-sight and soul-sight — distinguishing not the name but the instrument and reach. Both are genuine acts of perceiving; the root holds them together as two expressions of one faculty.

استنباط (inference): from the root ن-ب-ط, meaning to dig until water wells up from below. نَبَطَ is the water seeping from a freshly dug well; the Form X verb استنبط means to actively draw up what is hidden deep within. The root fits the argument perfectly: hidden truth is already present; the soul draws it to the surface.

نفس (soul): from the root ن-ف-س, meaning to breathe or exhale. نَفَس is a single breath. The soul (نفس) is the animating breath — the living, knowing principle within a person. This root connection suggests that the soul's perception is not an external act but something as intimate and continuous as breathing itself.

notes.body:
The entire grammatical argument pivots on what Arabic grammarians call **the lam of purpose** (لام الغاية). When لام precedes a noun in Arabic, it signals that the verb is directed toward that noun as its intended aim — a goal that lies ahead. If an action is aimed at a future occasion, the action must already be underway before that occasion arrives. This is one of the principal, documented functions of لام in the classical Arabic grammatical tradition.

No named grammarian is cited, but an authority just as weighty is invoked: the Prophet's own mastery of Arabic. He declared

أَنَا أَفْصَحُ الْعَرَبِ وَلَا فَخْرَ
"I am the most eloquent of the Arabs, and this is no boast."

Arabic already possesses clear temporal prepositions — عند meaning "at the moment of," and حين meaning "when" — that would have served if the intended sense were simply "begin fasting the instant you sight it." A speaker of that calibre does not reach for لام when عند would do, and that deliberate choice is itself **the grammatical proof**.

The three analogies demonstrate a consistent pattern in living Arabic usage:

- "Prepare things for his arrival" — the preparation is done before he arrives
- "Compose a poem for the meeting" — the poem is finished before the meeting begins
- "Work for the Hereafter" — the work is performed before the Hereafter comes

In each instance لام points toward a coming occasion, and the action must be complete or underway when that occasion is reached.

The opponent's counter-example —

أَقِمِ ٱلصَّلَوٰةَ لِدُلُوكِ ٱلشَّمْسِ
"Establish the prayer at the declining of the sun"
Al-Isra' 17:78

— does not trouble the argument at all. The true declining is perceived by **the soul's vision** before the eye registers it, so the لام there carries the same anticipatory logic: one should already be in prayer at the soul-perceived moment of the sun's decline.

The argument stops short of claiming this is the only grammatically permissible reading. Mainstream jurists read the same لام as a simple temporal marker and arrived at the opposite ruling. The case being made is rather that the purposive reading is **the more precise and fitting** for a speaker of supreme eloquence — and the only reading consistent with the broader proof that the vision of the soul is the nobler faculty of the two.

notes.quote: the sense of lam, as it is used and as it is intended, is that the act must precede that for which it is done
etymology: رؤية (sighting / vision): from the root ر-أ-ي, meaning to see. The same root gives رأي (considered opinion or view). The root already carries both physical sight and inward perception — one forms a رأي by seeing a truth with the mind. This dual life is what the argument exploits: the crescent's رؤية can be the eye's apprehension or the soul's knowing.

أفصح (most eloquent): from the root ف-ص-ح, meaning to be clear, pure, and unobstructed — like a spring running free of sediment. فصيح describes speech stripped of all obscurity. The superlative أفصح implies a speaker whose every word choice is exact, never careless, making the appeal to the Prophet's فصاحة a precision argument: if his language was exact, his choice of لام over عند was deliberate.

دلوك (the declining of the sun): from the root د-ل-ك, meaning to rub or press by friction. The sun's دلوك is the moment it rubs past the meridian, crossing from ascent into descent. The metaphor of friction conveys a precise threshold, not a gradual event — reinforcing the argument that دلوك marks an exact instant the soul perceives before the eye can register it.

غاية (goal / ultimate aim, as in لام الغاية): from the root غ-ي-ي, meaning the furthest point a thing reaches — its outermost limit or boundary. A غاية is not a midpoint; it is the utmost extent. As a grammatical label, it describes the لام's role exactly: it directs an action toward its furthest aim ahead, which by definition cannot yet have been reached when the action begins.
